reason: The scenario replays refresh1 immediately after it was rotated. Go treats any second presentation as reuse and revokes the family (400 invalid_grant); Rust's 10 s replay leeway reads it as the client racing itself and rotates it again into a sibling (200 with fresh tokens). A replay after the leeway is refused as reuse, as in Go.
ruling: owner decisions 2026-09-25, #21 (Java ruling 5): a refresh token rotated out less than 10 s ago rotates again into a sibling in the same family

reason: Consequence of the leeway on the step before: on Go that replay revoked the family, so refresh2 is refused (400 invalid_grant); on Rust the family was never revoked (the replay was within the leeway), so refresh2 still rotates (200). Refreshing a genuinely revoked family is refused on Rust too (see refresh-revoked).
ruling: owner decisions 2026-09-25, #21 (Java ruling 5): a refresh token rotated out less than 10 s ago rotates again into a sibling in the same family

reason: Rust's router-config document lists every queue the scheduler can publish to: both priorities for every tenant, and every client's tenant. Go lists a tenant only through a pool's or ACTIVE subscription's client_identifier (which no API sets) and HIGH_PRIORITY only where a subscription asks for it, so a client-scoped job, or one claiming HIGH_PRIORITY itself, lands on a queue no router consumes (delivery harness). The shape is Go's; only more queues are listed (docs/parity/go-route-gaps.md). queueUri also names each side's own database (parity_go / parity_rust).
ruling: owner decisions 2026-09-25, #31: Go's router-config omits client-scoped queues; Rust keeps the complete list
